But the record is thin and self-consciously undercounts, so silence is not safety (rule 3). Known negatives: a historic morality ordinance reported in force in one region (in-force status contested) carrying up to ten years; public-morality provisions reaching trans people; police documented arresting and torturing queer residents and banning LGBTQ organising; no non-discrimination or complaint route; very low social acceptance, with family/public abuse reported; HIV medication access precarious. The same-sex statute and resident-scoped enforcement are secondary (rule 2) and undated (rule 18), and the 12-person 2018 sample cannot establish trans-specific prevalence (rule 17). One step below acceptance-with-protections; a weak tier-2/strong tier-3 profile."}","refusal":null,"reasoning":"Let me work through this dossier carefully.

Key facts: two regional criminal-law regimes. One region: 1960 penal code derived from neighbour's 1951 revision — no criminalisation of consensual same-sex acts. Other region: contested whether 1936 ordinance criminalising same-sex conduct (up to 10 years) is in force. No prohibition on trans identity as such. But trans people can be caught by public-morality provisions (per advocacy project).

No legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protections (resident-facing — per rule 1, not directly traveller exposure, but absence of any non-discrimination complaint route is a climate signal).

Enforcement: police arrested and tortured gay residents; collaboration charges usual; two cases tried explicitly for homosexuality over an undated 3-year window. Police banned LGBTQ activity of a queer cultural organisation; wave of hate messages. Social/family persecution. Undated transphobic threats and attacks. HIV care access problems.

Deliberately not counted: entry/visa, passport markers, airport screening, bathroom access, detention placement, hate-crime provisions — all unsourced.

Also: blockaded region health system collapse since Oct 2023 — HIV medication difficult.

So what should the rating be? This is a thin-data jurisdiction with contested criminalisation in one region, documented police arrests and torture of gay residents (state's own hand, but described for residents — 'gay residents', though the mechanism — collaboration charges, morality policing — would reach visibly gender-nonconforming visitors), documented ban on LGBTQ organising, documented social hostility, and no trans-specific violence data.

The rubric says sexuality law is secondary; but here the dossier documents the lever being used: police arrests and torture, morality provisions, police banning LGBTQ activity. That's state-tolerated/state-directed targeting (tier 2) at least in one region. Plus no documented recourse whatsoever — no complaint mechanism, no anti-discrimination law.

Not tier 1 (no documented universal facility/custody/document exposure — explicitly unsourced). So per precedence ladder, worst documented feature is tier 2-ish: police arrests/torture of gay residents on collaboration grounds, undated; police ban on LGBTQ activity; social/family persecution with thin/no recourse. But the tier-2 evidence is largely resident-focused and undated.

Rule 20: activist visibility is not danger; local vulnerability is not traveller risk. Most of the violence/discrimination described is resident-sphere (family, public, HIV care). The visitor-facing sphere (borders, documents, facilities, custody) is explicitly unsourced. That argues against going very low.

But rule 3/13: thin-data extrapolation — don't default to midpoint. What structural signals? Contested criminalisation of same-sex conduct with up to 10 years in one region; state's police enforcing morality and torturing; no legal protections; no complaint route; documented hostility index low (130th). Absence of evidence — in a well-documented state silence would be mildly positive, but here the record is thin and explicitly acknowledges data gaps (HIV undercount, taboos hindering data collection), so silence is not evidence of safety.

Also relevant: the record explicitly says the country's situation involves contested legal status, and the "deliberately not counted" section lists many unknowns: entry procedures, gender markers, screening, facilities, custody. These are open questions — per rule 13, open questions are "far lighter" than known exposures, and not exposures at all.

Known exposures relevant to a traveller: 
- Public-morality provisions reaching trans people (per advocacy project) — state could use morality law against visible gender nonconformity.
- Police practice of arresting/torturing, collaboration charges — but described as against residents, in national-authority areas; a foreign trans visitor could plausibly be caught if discovered, though the described pattern is gay residents.
- Police banning LGBTQ organising — signals institutional hostility, and the ban plus hate messages shows state hostility toward queer visibility.
- Societal hostility (2018, 12-person sample; 130th on acceptance index, 2010-2020) — dated but consistent.
- HIV medication access problems, especially in the blockaded region — relevant to a traveller relying on medication continuity.

Severity if outed: contested criminal law (10 years) in one region; police violence/torture documented; state hostility. That's high severity. Probability of being outed: no documented border checks, but ID checks generally unknown; social visibility.

Comparing with anchors: 0.35 profiles have universal institutional exposure or documented police extortion/sweeps with failed recourse. 0.45 profiles have a current universal-exposure practice or discrimination at scale. 0.55 profiles have recurring visitor-facing harms with incomplete remedies. Here: no documented universal exposure reaching visitors, no documented trans-specific targeting of visitors; but a documented pattern of state police arresting and torturing queer residents, a morality-law lever that reaches trans people, an actual (contested) criminal statute with a 10-year penalty in one region, no recourse, and deep social stigma.

Hmm. The contested nature matters — rule 6: unenforced statute small factor; a statute with documented arrests large. The arrests documented are for homosexuality on collaboration charges, not for the 1936 ordinance per se; and it's undated. Actually the torture is described as ground for persecution usually a "collaboration charge" — so the arrests aren't under the sodomy law but a security law. Trans visitor exposure via that route: a foreigner is less likely targeted as a collaborator.

But the morality provisions — public morality provisions could reach trans people. Undocumented enforcement though.

I'd put this somewhere around 0.35-0.45. Let me think about which.

Rule 13's ladder: (1) state universal exposure — not documented. (2) state-tolerated/directed targeting — police extortion, raids, arrests for presentation — partially documented (arrests of gay residents, torture; morality provisions reaching trans people; police ban on organising) but not documented as reaching trans visitors, undated, and no raids on trans people described. (3) documented societal hostility with thin/no recourse — yes, documented (2018 sample; undated threats; acceptance index; family abuse; no complaint route). (4) dated/scattered incidents.

The worst documented feature for the traveller is somewhere between tier 3 and a weak tier 2: state hostility toward LGBTQ visibility (undated police ban, arrests/torture with undated account) plus societal hostility with no recourse. No documented universal-exposure measure.

Compared to 0.35 anchors: those all feature a documented active traveller-facing exposure with failed remedy. Here the traveller-facing exposure is largely inferred from resident-sphere evidence and undated enforcement, plus open questions on everything (borders, facilities, custody). The rubric says open questions are light, not exposures.

Compare to 0.45 anchors: each has a current universal-exposure practice or visitor-facing discrimination at scale without effective correction. Here the "discrimination at scale" is a 12-person 2018 survey of women — too thin per rule 17 (population/category/period mismatch: not trans-specific, dated). So 0.45's driver is arguably absent.

Compare to 0.55 anchors: recurring visitor-facing harms with incomplete remedies. Not documented here.

So maybe above 0.45 but below 0.55? Hmm, but consider the state hostility: police banning LGBTQ activity, torturing residents. That's more severe than what's in 0.55 profiles. But it's resident-scoped and undated.

Let me weigh: the criminal statute in one region (contested, 10 years) is a real severity signal — a trans woman travelling with a male partner, or a trans person caught by public-morality provisions, faces a potential 10-year penalty. But contested in-force status reduces weight; still, two international HR orgs hold it in force and a regional advocacy project lists it as in force. Per rule 6, a statute with no documented arrests under it = modest weight. But there is documented enforcement of morality generally.

Also: no legal gender recognition at all, so a trans visitor's documents come from home — not directly relevant. No anti-discrimination route — climate signal.

I think a score around 0.40 seems right: between 0.35 and 0.45. Let me reconsider whether higher.

Arguments for higher (safer, e.g., 0.45-0.50): no documented trans-specific offence anywhere; no documented trans-specific enforcement or violence counts; no documented visitor-facing facility, custody, or border restriction; public organising existed (queer organisations exist, cross-border); the state has legislated neither for nor against (ambiguity cuts toward no active campaign); the trans-exposure is via morality provisions only, silence suggests general hostility rather than targeting.

Arguments for lower (e.g., 0.30-0.35): one region has a contested but reported-in-force sodomy statute with 10-year penalty; state police documented arresting and torturing LGBT residents, and imposing a ban on LGBTQ organizing; social acceptance very low (130th); no anti-discrimination or complaint recourse of any kind; medication access issues; flight/refugee flows documented (90 people fleeing violence); thin data with known undercounts, so silence isn't safety.

Rule 13 caution: "a KNOWN traveler-facing exposure is the heaviest input; an OPEN QUESTION ... far lighter; absence of resident-facing machinery lightest of all. A latent tangential statute plus open questions plus thin formal recourse hold the jurisdiction a step below the acceptance-with-protections tier — a step, not a tier."

So: latent tangential statute (the 1936 ordinance, contested, plus 2003 draft unknown) + open questions (borders, facilities, custody, documents) + thin formal recourse (no anti-discrimination, no LGR) → one step below the acceptance-with-protections tier. The acceptance-with-protections tier... in the 0.65-0.75 region. A step below would be ~0.55-0.60? Hmm, that reading would be too generous — but that framework assumes comparable social acceptance; here we have documented social hostility and state hostility, so more deductions.

But also there's documented state-directed persecution of queer people — police torture — which is a tier-2 feature, not just "latent statute". Though scoped to residents.

I think 0.40 is a reasonable landing point: High/Elevated boundary. Actually 0.40 is the boundary between High Risk and Elevated Risk.

Let me think about the 0.35 anchors again. 0.35-A: universal bathroom ban with document checks, courts rejecting complaints, no exemption for visitors, emergency wards same rule. That's a hard tier-1 universal exposure, plus official framing of trans as threats. That gets 0.35. 0.35-C: police routinely stop visibly trans people, photograph passports, demand payments, documented including foreign travellers, with no discipline. That's tier-2 state targeting of visitors — 0.35.

Our dossier: no documented policing of trans visitors; contested statute in one region; documented police torture of gay residents (undated, resident-scoped); police ban on queer organising; deep social stigma; no recourse. That seems less severe than a documented universal facility ban or routine police extortion of trans travellers. But the potential criminal penalty (10 years) plus documented police torture raises severity if discovered. And rule 3: absence of documented visitor-facing incidents in a thin-data state is not safety.

I'd say ~0.38-0.42. Let me pick 0.40. Hmm, but consider whether the documued evidence of state torture of queer residents plus a 10-year criminal statute should push lower, into 0.30-0.35. The rubric warns against letting sexuality law dominate and against letting resident-sphere material drive visitor ratings. Also the enforcement evidence is undated and doesn't establish present frequency.

I'll go with 0.40, explaining: undocumented trans-specific visitor exposure, but a reported-in-force (contested) sodomy statute in one region carrying 10 years, documented police persecution of queer residents and a ban on queer organising, no anti-discrimination or complaint recourse, low social acceptance, and a care-access gap — with all visitor-facing mechanics (borders, facilities, custody) unresolved so not counted. That places it at the top of High Risk / bottom of Elevated.

Actually, let me reconsider whether to go a bit lower, like 0.35. The distinguishing feature vs. 0.35 anchors: those have an active documented traveller-facing exposure. Ours has a statute whose in-force status is contested and whose enforcement is contested, plus documented state violence against residents. Rule 3 (burden of proof symmetry): documented negatives count — the torture account and the organizing ban are documented negatives, even if resident-scoped and undated. That plus deep stigma and zero recourse pushes down. But the rubric repeatedly warns against resident-sphere material. The trans-specific content is: public-morality provisions reach trans people; undated transphobic threats/attacks; no LGR/discrimination protections (climate only); HIV care access.

I'll settle on 0.38. Hmm, need decisiveness. Differences between 0.35 and 0.40 are minor. I'll say 0.40.
